extracted.intended_audience: natural philosophers / observational scientists (members/readers of the Royal Society); readers of 17th-century natural-history and astronomical reports
extracted.subtask_description: Writing and reporting empirical natural-history and astronomical observations and anatomical dissections, including measurements, specimen handling, figures, and comparison with prior authorities. Emphasis on precise timings, instrument use, and cautious interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record precise times of observation
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give exact times (hours, minutes, seconds where possible) and note the timekeeping method used; examples in the text include lines such as 'Time by the watch', 'at 9h.', 'at the hour of 10 in the morning', and tabulated times for occultations. Precise timing allows determination of conjunctions and sequence of events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use calibrated instruments and state measurement method
rubrics_metrics.description: the distances being sometimes taken with the micrometer
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report which instruments were used (micrometer, watch, etc.) and when different methods were applied. Specify how distances/angles were measured and any instrument settings so others can evaluate precision and repeat measurements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide repeated observations to show temporal trends
rubrics_metrics.description: the continual increase of distance observed on the following: days ... decreased till May 18, and after that continually increased
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record observations on multiple dates and times to reveal trends (e.g., decreasing then increasing distance). Tabulate serial measurements so readers can infer events like conjunctions from the trend.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare observations with established predictions and catalogues
rubrics_metrics.description: which, according to the compilers of the almanacs, ought not to have happened till the 26th ... The small star A is not in Tycho's catalogue; but in my new one it is called ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-reference observations with almanacs, star catalogues, and prior authorities; note agreements or discrepancies (e.g., predicted vs observed conjunction dates, presence/absence in a catalogue). This situates new observations within existing knowledge and highlights novelties or errors in prior sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include illustrative figures and plates for microscopic or detailed structures
rubrics_metrics.description: they are represented to the best of my skill in fig. 12, pi. 18, where ABC is an animalcule ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide drawings/plates (labelled figures) to accompany descriptions, especially for microscopic bodies or unusual anatomical features. Reference figures in the text so readers can see the phenomena being described.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe specimen handling, preparation, and preservation
rubrics_metrics.description: I cut open the testicles ... kept so long before I had it for dissection, it was rendered less fit for such inquiries
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State how specimens were obtained, prepared, and how long they were kept before examination; indicate any conditions (salt, urine contamination, delay) that might affect the observations or their reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide quantitative measurements and dimensions
rubrics_metrics.description: from the end of the body ... was 1 feet 2 inches; ... the colon ... measured Q feet in length; ... 27 feet of these intestines
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give linear dimensions, counts, and other quantitative data with units. Where possible, provide multiple measurements (e.g., lengths, circumferences, counts of lobes) so anatomical structures can be compared and reproduced.

rubrics_metrics.name: State sample size and limit generalizations from single specimens
rubrics_metrics.description: it being the only one of the kind I have dissected; I know not how far it may be preternatural, or to be met with again
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Declare how many specimens were examined and caution readers against generalizing from solitary or atypical specimens. Explicitly consider whether observed features may be singular/pathological (preternatural) versus typical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish observation from conjecture and hypothesis
rubrics_metrics.description: The reason that I give for it is, that many of the eggs in the ovarium have each of them received an animalcule ... I judge the bodies of the animalcules to have been of the thickness ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clearly separate what was directly observed from the author's interpretations or proposed explanations. Use wording that indicates judgment or hypothesis ('I judge', 'the reason I give') so readers can assess evidence versus inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimate counts and abundances and explain estimation method
rubrics_metrics.description: The number of animalcules in all the seed was so great, that I judge there might be 10,000 of them to one of the female's eggs ... 40 might be in the space of a sand ... not less than 1000 of the third sort in the space of a sand
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When exact counts are impractical, provide reasoned numerical estimates, describe how they were approximated (e.g., by area, by sight), and give context so readers can judge their plausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use comparative anatomy and cite prior authorities
rubrics_metrics.description: Such numerous rings I have since met with in the filaments of the muscle of a lamb ... What Dr. Tyson in his anatomical description falls, according to Buffon, into a very material error ... Falco-burgius says ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare new anatomical findings with descriptions by earlier anatomists (Grew, Malpighi, de Graaf, Buffon, Falco-burgius). Cite these authorities and note points of agreement or disagreement to situate results within existing literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report units, coordinate/directional measures, and angular notation explicitly
rubrics_metrics.description: d. h. m. pts. ... 28' 30" ... 12' 10" ... parts of the micrometer ... 19° 11' 36"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State the units used (degrees, minutes, seconds, parts, feet, inches) and provide consistent notation for angles and positions. When using specialized measures (micrometer parts), explain their relation to conventional units if possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain omissions and editorial choices
rubrics_metrics.description: The observations on digestion and on the motion of the blood in a fever are omitted, as being irreconcilable with subsequent physiological discoveries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When material is omitted (e.g., because later findings contradict it), explicitly state the reason so readers understand scope and editorial decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relate structure to function where appropriate and offer mechanistic interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: From the indentings of these filaments I can not only satisfy myself how the limbs come to stand bent, when the muscles are at rest, but also why we can walk a longer time than stand still
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Go beyond description to infer functional significance of structures, but mark these inferences clearly and support them with observed structural details or comparative examples.
